title: The Red Notebook
teaser: Hassan writes rhymes on the metro. Tonight he has to say them out loud.
paragraphs: Hassan is nineteen and works in a phone shop in Shubra. Every day, he takes the metro to work. While other people look at their phones, Hassan writes in a small red notebook. He writes rhymes about his street, his friends and his dreams.
Nobody knows about the notebook. Hassan is shy. When his friends rap in the street at night, he only listens. His words stay on paper.

One evening, his friend Tarek sees the notebook in his bag. He reads one page and his eyes go wide. “Bro, this is better than anything I write,” he says. “There is an open mic on Thursday. You have to come.”
On Thursday, the small café is full and loud. Hassan’s heart beats fast. When the host calls his name, his mouth is dry. He looks at the crowd, and for a moment he wants to run away.

Then he closes his eyes and imagines the metro: the noise, the people, the red notebook on his knee. He starts to rap, slowly at first, then faster. When he finishes, the café is silent for one second. Then everyone starts to clap and shout. Tarek is the loudest.

targets.en: words that end with the same sound
nervous about talking to other people
the person who presents a show or event
a large group of people
to make a picture in your mind

questions.q: Where does Hassan write his rhymes?
Why does nobody know about the notebook?
What does Tarek tell him to do?
What does “shy” mean?

recap: Shy Hassan writes rhymes on the metro; his friend Tarek finds the notebook and brings him to an open mic, where the crowd loves him.

title: Old Songs Inside New Beats: What Is Sampling?
teaser: That piano loop you love might be fifty years old.
paragraphs: Listen carefully to many hip-hop songs and you will hear something surprising: a few seconds of an old soul record, a jazz piano or even a film soundtrack, repeated again and again. This is called sampling, and it is one of the foundations of hip-hop.

Sampling started in New York in the 1970s. DJs at block parties noticed that people danced most during the short drum breaks in funk records. So they used two copies of the same record on two turntables and played the break again and again. Later, machines called samplers made it possible to record any sound and play it back with a button.

A producer might take a short piece of music, change its speed, cut it into smaller parts and rearrange them. Sometimes the original is easy to recognise; sometimes it is so changed that only experts notice. Producers often search old markets and online archives for forgotten records nobody else has used.

But sampling has a legal side. The original recording and the song itself belong to someone. Today, artists usually need permission and must pay the owners, a process called clearing a sample. If they do not, they can be taken to court.

Because clearing samples can be expensive, some producers now hire musicians to play new music that sounds old, or they use free sample libraries. Either way, the idea remains the same: building something new on top of the music that came before.

targets.en: the base that something is built on
to put things in a different order
to know something because you saw or heard it before
a collection of old records or documents
when someone says you are allowed to do something
to pay someone to work for you

questions.q: Where did sampling start?
Why did DJs repeat drum breaks?

options: Getting permission and paying the owners

questions.q: What do some producers do because clearing is expensive?
options: Hire musicians to play new music that sounds old
questions.ar: بعض المنتجين بيعملوا إيه بسبب التكلفة؟

recap: Sampling began with DJs looping drum breaks in 1970s New York; producers reuse old recordings but must usually get permission and pay.

title: One Million Views
teaser: Salma sang in her kitchen. The internet was listening.
paragraphs: Salma is sixteen and lives in Mansoura. She loves pop music and sings all the time: in the shower, in the kitchen, on the way to school. Her mother sometimes says, “Please, Salma, five minutes of quiet!”

One evening, she records herself singing an English pop song with her old guitar. The kitchen light is bad, and you can hear the neighbour’s TV. But her voice is soft and clear. She uploads the video and goes to sleep.

In the morning, her phone will not stop buzzing. The video has fifty thousand views. By the evening, it has five hundred thousand. People share it and write, “What a voice!” A few people write mean comments too, and those hurt.
Salma’s English teacher, Miss Dina, sees the video. She tells Salma, “Read the good comments twice and the bad ones once. Then close the app and practise.”

A week later, the video passes one million views. Salma is happy, but she is also tired of her phone. She turns it off, picks up her guitar and starts writing her own song. It is in Arabic and English, and it is about her kitchen.

to send something to other people

options: Read good comments twice and bad ones once

questions.q: What does Salma do at the end?

recap: Salma’s kitchen cover video gets one million views; her teacher helps her deal with comments and she starts writing her own song.

title: Why a Song Gets Stuck in Your Head
teaser: Scientists call it an earworm. Here is how to get rid of one.
paragraphs: You hear a song once in a taxi, and for the next three days it plays in your head again and again. Scientists call this an earworm, and studies suggest that most people experience one at least once a week.

Earworms usually come from songs with a few common features. They often have a simple, repetitive melody, a slightly unusual jump between notes, and a fast or steady rhythm. Pop producers know this, so many hits are built around a short hook that repeats many times.

Your memory also plays a role. Often, the earworm is not the whole song but only a short part, usually the chorus. Some researchers think that the brain keeps replaying the part because it is incomplete, like an unfinished task that keeps returning to your mind.
Earworms are more likely when you are tired, stressed or doing something automatic, such as walking or washing dishes. In these moments, your mind wanders, and familiar music fills the empty space.

How do you stop one? Studies offer a few strange but useful ideas: listen to the whole song to the end, chew gum, or do a task that needs your full attention, like a puzzle. Some people simply choose a different song to replace it, which works until the new song gets stuck instead.

targets.en: to have something happen to you
a typical part or quality of something
saying or doing the same thing many times
not finished
done without thinking
to put something new in the place of something else

questions.q: What is an earworm?
options: A song stuck in your head

questions.q: Which part of a song usually gets stuck?
options: A short part, usually the chorus

questions.q: When are earworms more likely?
options: When you are tired or doing something automatic

questions.q: Which is a tip to stop one?

recap: Earworms are short catchy parts of songs that replay in the head, especially when tired; listening to the end or a puzzle can help.

title: The Wedding DJ
teaser: The speakers stopped working. Three hundred guests were waiting.
paragraphs: Mido is a wedding DJ in Imbaba. Every weekend, he carries his speakers and his laptop to a different wedding. He knows exactly which song makes the aunties dance and which one makes the young men jump.

Tonight is a big wedding on a rooftop. There are three hundred guests, colourful lights and a huge cake. The bride and groom are about to make their entrance. Mido presses play, and suddenly… silence. The speakers are dead.
Everyone looks at him. The groom’s father looks very angry. Mido checks the cables, but his hands are shaking. Then he sees the problem: the power cable is burnt.

His little cousin, Bebo, is helping him tonight. Bebo runs down six floors to the shop on the corner and comes back with a new cable. While they fix it, Mido has an idea. He picks up a tabla and starts to play a simple rhythm. The guests start clapping with him.

Two minutes later, the speakers come back to life. Mido plays the loudest song he has, and the bride and groom walk in. The groom’s father is dancing now. After the wedding, he gives Mido a big tip and says, “Next wedding, you are our DJ.”

targets.en: a person you invite to an event
the moment someone comes in
a wire that carries electricity
damaged by fire or heat
extra money you give for good service

questions.q: What is Mido’s job?

What did Mido do while they fixed it?
A “tip” is…

recap: At a rooftop wedding Mido’s speakers die; his cousin gets a new cable while Mido keeps the guests clapping, and the night is saved.

title: How a Street Sound Went Global
teaser: From cheap laptops in Cairo’s side streets to festival stages abroad.
paragraphs: Mahraganat, which means “festivals”, is a style of electronic street music that grew in the working-class neighbourhoods of Cairo in the late 2000s. It mixes the energy of traditional wedding music with electronic beats, heavy bass and voices changed by software.

What made it possible was cheap technology. Young people did not need studios or record companies. With a used laptop, free or cracked software and a microphone, they could make songs in their bedrooms. They shared them on CDs, through mobile phones and later on YouTube and SoundCloud.

The style was born at weddings and street parties, so it is made for dancing. The lyrics often talk about everyday life: friendship, betrayal, money problems and love, usually with humour and a lot of slang.

Not everyone welcomed it. Some critics said the lyrics were rude and the music was noisy, and at times there were attempts to ban certain performers. But the audience kept growing, and many songs reached hundreds of millions of views.

Today, mahraganat beats can be heard in films, adverts and even at festivals in Europe. For many fans abroad, it is their first contact with Egyptian music. Its story shows how a sound created with almost nothing can travel around the world.

recap: Mahraganat grew in Cairo’s streets thanks to cheap laptops; despite critics it reached millions of fans and international stages.

title: Four Friends and a Garage
teaser: Their first show had nine people. Two were their mothers.
paragraphs: Four friends from Heliopolis started a band in a garage. Laila plays the guitar, Fady plays the drums, Sherine plays the bass and Kareem sings. They call the band Blue Balcony.
They practise every Friday. The garage is hot and small, and the neighbours often complain about the noise. Fady puts old blankets on the walls to make it quieter. It helps a little.

After six months, they play their first show in a small café. Only nine people come. Two of them are Laila’s and Kareem’s mothers. Kareem forgets the words of the second song. Everyone laughs, and he laughs too.

They do not stop. They record their songs on a phone and post them online. They play in cafés, at university events and at a friend’s birthday. Slowly, people start to know their songs and sing along.

One year later, Blue Balcony plays at a small music festival. There are four hundred people in front of the stage. Before they start, Kareem looks at his friends and says, “Remember the garage?” Fady hits the drums, and the crowd screams.

targets.en: a group of musicians
to say that you are not happy about something
a thick cover for a bed
the high place where people perform

questions.q: Where does the band practise?

recap: Four friends form the band Blue Balcony in a garage; after a tiny first show they keep playing and reach a festival a year later.

title: What Does a Mixing Engineer Do?
teaser: Same song, same players — why does one version sound so much better?
paragraphs: When a band records a song, each instrument and voice is usually recorded on its own track. A simple rock song can easily have thirty tracks: several for the drums, two for the guitars, one for the bass, and many for the vocals. Mixing is the art of turning all these tracks into one balanced piece of music.

The first job of a mixing engineer is volume. Every track needs the right level, so that the vocals are clear but the drums still feel powerful. This sounds easy, but a small change can completely change the mood of a song.

Next comes equalisation, or EQ. Every sound has low, middle and high frequencies. If the bass guitar and the kick drum both have a lot of low frequencies, they fight each other and the song sounds muddy. The engineer removes a little from one to make space for the other.

The engineer also places each sound in space. Panning moves a guitar slightly to the left or right speaker. Reverb adds the feeling of a room, from a small bedroom to a huge hall. Compression controls the difference between quiet and loud parts so the performance feels more even.

Finally, the mixed song goes to mastering, where another engineer prepares it to sound good on every system, from cheap earphones to big club speakers. Good mixing is often invisible: when it is done well, listeners simply feel that the song sounds right.

title: The Oud on the Wall
teaser: Grandpa’s oud was silent for years. Then Amira took it down.
paragraphs: In Amira’s grandmother’s flat in Old Cairo, there is an old oud on the wall. It belonged to Amira’s grandfather. He played it every evening on the balcony. After he died, nobody touched it.
Amira is fifteen. One summer afternoon, she asks her grandmother, “Can I take it down?” Her grandmother is surprised, but she nods. The oud is dusty, and two strings are broken.

Amira takes it to a music shop on Mohamed Ali Street. The old man in the shop holds it carefully. “This is a very good oud,” he says. “It was made by hand, maybe sixty years ago.” He changes the strings and shows her how to tune it.
Every day, Amira practises. Her fingers hurt and the sounds are not beautiful. She watches lessons online and plays very slowly. Her grandmother listens from the kitchen and does not say anything.

One evening, Amira sits on the balcony and plays a simple old melody. Her grandmother comes out and sits next to her. She closes her eyes. “Your grandfather played this one,” she says quietly. Then she starts to sing.

targets.en: a thin wire on an instrument that makes sound

to make an instrument play the right notes

recap: Amira repairs her late grandfather’s oud, practises every day, and plays an old melody that makes her grandmother sing.

title: Maqam: The Secret Map of Arabic Music
teaser: Why does Arabic music sound so different from Western pop?
paragraphs: If you play a Western pop song and a classic Arabic song one after the other, even without any musical training you can hear that they are built differently. One important reason is the maqam system.

A maqam (plural: maqamat) is a set of notes and rules for moving between them. It is similar to a scale in Western music, but it is more than a list of notes. Each maqam has typical melodies, a starting note, important notes to rest on, and a special feeling that musicians and listeners recognise.

Many maqamat use notes that do not exist on a piano. Western music divides the octave into twelve equal steps, but Arabic music also uses notes that sit between them, often called quarter tones. Instruments like the oud have no frets, so players can find these notes easily with their fingers.

Each maqam is connected to a mood. Maqam Rast is often described as proud and balanced, Bayati as warm and close to everyday life, and Saba as sad and emotional. In a long performance, a skilled musician moves from one maqam to another, a technique called modulation, and takes the audience on an emotional journey.

Learning the maqamat takes years, and traditionally it was taught by ear, from teacher to student. But even a beginner can start by listening carefully: try to notice when a song suddenly changes colour. Often, that is the moment the maqam changes.

recap: Arabic music uses maqamat: note sets with rules, quarter tones and moods; musicians move between them to create emotional journeys.

title: A Poem on the Wall
teaser: Every morning, a new line appeared on the old wall. Who was writing them?
paragraphs: On Laila’s way to school in Dokki, there is an old grey wall. One Monday morning, she sees a line of poetry on it, written in white chalk: “The city is loud, but the sky is quiet.”

On Tuesday, there is a new line under it. On Wednesday, another one. The lines are short and simple, but they are beautiful. Some are in Arabic and some are in English. People stop, read and take photos.
Laila wants to know who the poet is. On Thursday, she leaves home very early. It is still dark. She waits behind a tree near the wall.
At six o’clock, an old man comes with a bag. He is the street cleaner. Laila sees him every day, but she never noticed him. He takes a piece of chalk from his pocket and writes slowly.

Laila walks to him. “Are you the poet?” she asks. He smiles and looks a little shy. “I am just a man who sweeps the street,” he says. “But I have a lot of time to think.” The next morning, under his new line, Laila writes her first line of poetry.

title: Spoken Word: Poetry You Perform
teaser: It’s not rap and it’s not a speech. So what is it?
paragraphs: Spoken word is poetry that is written to be performed out loud, usually in front of an audience. While a printed poem lives on the page, a spoken word poem lives in the voice, the pauses and the body of the performer.

It has roots in many traditions. Ancient poets in many cultures, including Arab poets at markets and gatherings, recited their poems from memory. In the twentieth century, poets in the United States read with jazz musicians, and later poetry slams turned performance into a friendly competition.

At a poetry slam, poets usually have about three minutes. Judges chosen from the audience give scores, and the crowd reacts loudly. Because of the time limit and the live audience, spoken word poems are often personal, direct and emotional. They might talk about identity, family, injustice or love.

Spoken word uses many of the tools of rap, such as rhythm, repetition and rhyme, but it does not need a beat, and the rhythm can change freely. Performers use silence powerfully: a long pause before an important line can be more effective than shouting.

If you want to try it, start small. Write about something you know well, read it out loud many times, and notice where you want to breathe or slow down. Many cities have open mic nights where beginners are welcome, and the audience is usually supportive.
